passage: When I moved to Berlin for my degree, I smiled at everyone on the train, the way I would in my town at home. Nobody smiled back. A man frowned; a woman looked at her shoes. I decided the city was cold and felt lonely. My classmate Dolma, who grew up in a hill town and had studied in Japan first, laughed when I told her. "Here, smiling at strangers is odd," she said. "In Japan, when I bumped into someone I smiled to say sorry, and I was embarrassed, and people knew that. It changes place to place." I started watching what locals did instead of guessing. Now I nod to neighbours, and they nod back. - Sahil

qa.q: Which city did Sahil move to for the degree?
qa.a: Sahil moved to Berlin for the degree.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when nobody smiled back on the train?
qa.a: Sahil felt lonely and decided the city was cold, though the lack of smiles was really about local norms.

qa.q: What did Sahil change after talking to Dolma?
qa.a: Sahil started watching what locals did instead of guessing, and began nodding to neighbours.

qa.q: How might the man who frowned have seen Sahil's smile?
qa.a: He may have found it unusual from a stranger, not unfriendly, since smiling at strangers is odd there.

grounding: A student in a new city finds smiling at strangers means different things in different places, so local norms matter.

passage: Advisor's note. Usha, an exchange student from Manila, met me today after her professor complained that she "smiled and seemed not to care" about a missed deadline. When I asked Usha, she looked at her hands and said that in her family a smile is what you do when you feel embarrassed or want to say sorry, and she had been mortified. Here, the professor read her smile as being casual. I explained to Usha that many professors in this city expect an eye-contact apology in words. I also suggested she tell the professor directly that she was sorry. She agreed to write an email tonight. I will check in with her on Friday. - Vishal

qa.a: Usha is an exchange student from Manila.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she smiled about the missed deadline?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and mortified and meant the smile as a sorry, not as not caring.

qa.q: What did Vishal suggest Usha do?
qa.a: Vishal suggested Usha tell the professor directly in words that she was sorry, by email.

qa.q: How did the professor read Usha's smile?
qa.a: The professor read it as casual and uncaring, because in local norms a smile isn't usually an apology.

grounding: A student in a new place finds that a smile can cover embarrassment or apology, and local norms matter more than assumptions.
